## Background & Literature (tbc)

## **Research Goal**

This use case will quantify uncertainty in the coefficient of determination, $R^2$, by treating it as a function of the joint correlation matrix $R$:

$$
R^2 = R_{XY}^{T}R_{XX}^{-1}R_{XY}
$$

We will propagate uncertainty in the estimated joint correlation matrix $\hat R$ to uncertainty in $R^2(\hat R)$, and evaluate how this uncertainty changes across sample size, signal strength, and conditioning of the predictor correlation structure $R_{XX}$.

## Methods

We will study uncertainty in the coefficient of determination, $R^2$, by treating it as a function of the joint correlation matrix of $(Y, X)$. For standardized variables, the population $R^2$ can be written as

$$
R^2(R) = R_{XY}^{T}R_{XX}^{-1}R_{XY},
$$

where $R_{XX}$ is the predictor correlation matrix and $R_{XY}$ is the vector of correlations between the predictors and the outcome. This formula allows uncertainty in the estimated joint correlation matrix $\hat R$ to be propagated directly to uncertainty in $R^2$.

For each simulation scenario, we will first specify a population predictor correlation matrix $R_{XX}$, a coefficient vector $\beta$, and a target population value $R^2_{\text{true}}$. The data-generating model is

$$
Y = X^T\beta + \varepsilon,
\qquad
X \sim N(0, R_{XX}),
\qquad
\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2),
$$

with $X \perp \varepsilon$. Given $R_{XX}$ and $\beta$, the variance of signal ( $X^T \beta$ ) is

$$
S = \beta^T R_{XX}\beta.
$$

The error variance $\sigma^2$ will be chosen to achieve the target population $R^2$:

$$
\sigma^2 =
S\left(
\frac{1 - R^2_{\text{true}}}{R^2_{\text{true}}}
\right).
$$

This design allows scenarios with different predictor correlation structures and signal patterns to be compared at the same overall level of explanatory strength.

For each generated dataset, we will estimate the empirical joint correlation matrix

$$
\hat R = \operatorname{Cor}(Y, X),
$$

with block structure

$$
\hat R =
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat R_{YY} & \hat R_{YX} \\
\hat R_{XY} & \hat R_{XX}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The observed coefficient of determination will be computed as

$$
\hat R^2 =
\hat R_{XY}^{T}
\hat R_{XX}^{-1}
\hat R_{XY}.
$$

To quantify uncertainty, we will generate a 95% reverse-containment perturbation cloud of plausible joint correlation matrices around $\hat R$ using our MCMC approach:

$$
\left\{
\hat R^{(b)}
\right\}_{b=1}^{B},
\qquad B = 20{,}000.
$$

For each perturbed matrix, we will compute

$$
R^{2(b)}
=
\hat R_{XY}^{(b)T}
\left(
\hat R_{XX}^{(b)}
\right)^{-1}
\hat R_{XY}^{(b)}.
$$

We will summarize this distribution of $R^2$ using mean, median, min, max, and interval width. Histograms will also be used to visualize the distribution of $R^2$.

### Calibration

We will repeat $M$ times the above simulation (set $M=200$ ). Across repeated simulation replicates, we will evaluate calibration by comparing the nominal 95% perturbation intervals with the known population value $R^2_{\text{true}}$. Empirical coverage will be computed as

$$
\text{Empirical coverage}
=
\frac{1}{M}
\sum_{m=1}^{M}
\mathbf{1}
\left\{
R^2_{\text{true}} \in [L_m, U_m]
\right\},
$$

where $[L_m, U_m]$ is the min and max of $R^2$ from replicate $m$. The mean interval width will be computed as

$$
\text{Mean interval width}
=
\frac{1}{M}
\sum_{m=1}^{M}
(U_m - L_m).
$$

### Simulation Design: Specifying $R_{XX}$, $\beta$, Target $R^2$, and $n$

The simulation scenarios will vary the predictor correlation structure $R_{XX}$, coefficient vector $\beta$, and the target population $R^2$. These factors determine the population joint correlation structure and therefore the corresponding mapping to $R^2 = R_{XY}^T R_{XX}^{-1} R_{XX}$

The predictor correlation matrix $R_{XX}$ determines the geometry of the predictor space. We consider an AR(1) structure,

$$
(R_{XX})_{ij} = \rho^{|i-j|},
$$

where $\rho \in \{0.2, 0.5, 0.8\}$, representing weak, moderate, and strong predictor correlation. Larger values of $\rho$ induce stronger collinearity among nearby predictors, making $R_{XX}$ more ill-conditioned, leading $R_{XX}^{-1}$ to be more sensitive to perturbations.

The coefficient vector $\beta$ determines how the signal is distributed across the predictor space. Different $\beta$ scenarios will be evaluated since $R^2$ is determined by the signal quantity $\beta^T R_{XX}\beta$, not only on the magnitude of individual coefficients. When predictors are correlated, the same coefficient size can contribute differently to $R^2$ depending on whether the signal is concentrated among highly correlated predictors, spread (evenly) across predictors, or having flipped signs.

To compare scenarios at the same level of overall explanatory strength, we will specify target values of $R^2_{\text{true}}$ and choose $\sigma^2$ accordingly. Sample size $n \in (200, 500, 1000)$ will be

Table 1: Specification of different signal scenarios

| Signal scenario | Signal pattern | Example $\beta$ structure | Purpose |
|----------------|------------------|------------------|--------------------|
| S1 | All strong signals | $\beta_j = 0.6$ for all signal predictors | Evaluates uncertainty in $R^2$ when the signal is strong and distributed across predictors |
| S2 | All weak signals | $\beta_j = 0.2$ for all signal predictors | Evaluates whether weak distributed signals lead to wider uncertainty in $R^2$ |
| S3 | Mixed weak and strong signals | Some $\beta_j = 0.6$, others $\beta_j = 0.2$ | Evaluates how heterogeneous signal strength affects uncertainty in $R^2$ |
| S4 | One strong signal, otherwise weak | One $\beta_j = 0.8$, others $\beta_j = 0.2$ | Evaluates whether a dominant predictor stabilizes $R^2$, especially under correlated predictors |
| S5 | Positive/negative sign flip | $\beta_j$ alternates between $+0.4$ and $-0.4$ | Evaluates cancellation effects and whether opposing signals increase uncertainty in $R^2$ |

### Simulation Design: Specification of $R_{XX}$ and $\beta$

Because $R^2 = R_{XY}^{T} R_{XX}^{-1} R_{XY}$, uncertainty in $R^2$ is driven by both the predictor correlation structure $R_{XX}$ and the predictor-outcome correlation vector $R_{XY}$. The matrix $R_{XX}$ determines the geometry of the predictor space. When $R_{XX}$ is ill-conditioned, small perturbations in the estimated correlation matrix can lead to large changes in $R_{XX}^{-1}$, and therefore large changes in $R^2$. This corresponds to multicollinearity in multiple linear regression. In this simulation, we consider $R_{XX}$ using the AR(1) correlation structure, with a starting correlation $\rho$ being specified. This structure represent nearby predictors are more strongly correlated, while predictors farther apart are less correlated. For example, a $R_{XX}$ structure with $p=5$ is as follows:

$$
R_{XX} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \rho & \rho^2 & \rho^3 & \rho^4 \\
\rho & 1 & \rho & \rho^2 & \rho^3 \\
\rho^2 & \rho & 1 & \rho & \rho^2 \\
\rho^3 & \rho^2 & \rho & 1 & \rho \\
\rho^4 & \rho^3 & \rho^2 & \rho & 1
\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $(R_{XX})_{ij} = \rho^{|i-j|}$.

The vector $R_{XY}$ captures the association between the outcome $Y$ and predictors $X$. Under the data-generating model $Y = X^T\beta + \varepsilon$, $R_{XY}$ is induced by both $R_{XX}$ and $\beta$. Therefore, $\beta$ controls both the the strength and direction of the signal. This is important because the same signal strength can produce different levels of $R^2$, depending on the the structure of $R_{XX}$. For example, when predictors are correlated, the same coefficient size can contribute differently to $R^2$, depending on whether those nonzero coefficients are among independent predictors, highly correlated predictors, or predictors with opposite sign of effects. Therefore, varying $\beta$ allow us to investigate whether the uncertainty in $R^2$ is driven mainly by signal strength, signal direction, or interaction between the signal and the correlation structure.

### Simulation Procedure

In this simulation, different scenarios will be designed by varying $R_{XX}$ and $\beta$ (steps 1 to 2). Each scenario will then be repeated using different sample size to derive finite-sample estimate $\hat{R}$ (steps 3-5). Next, a 95% reverse containment samples of $\hat{R}$ will be generated using our MCMC approach (step 6). Lastly, we will map $R \mapsto R^2$ using $R^2 = R_{XY}^{T} R_{XX}^{-1} R_{XY}$ (step 7).

1.  Specify $\beta$, coefficients of each predictor, referring to table below.

2.  Specify $R_{XX}$, the predictor correlation structure among predictors using AR1 structure $$
    (R_{XX})_{ij} = \rho^{|i-j|},
    $$

    where $\rho \in \{0.2, 0.5, 0.8\}$, representing weak, moderate, and strong predictor correlation. Each signal scenario will be evaluated under all three correlation levels.

3.  Generate $n$ observations from $X \sim N(0, R_{XX})$.

4.  Derive outcome $Y = X^T \beta + \varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon \sim \ Norm(0,\sigma^2)$.

    [How to choose $\sigma^2$? Fixed value for]{style="color:red"}$\sigma^2$ [or work backwards from a given $R^2$?]{style="color:red"}

5.  Estimate the empirical joint correlation matrix: $\hat{R} = Cor(Y, X)$. $\hat{R}$ will be served as the starting point for the MCMC perturbation procedure.

6.  Perturb $\hat{R}$ using MCMC approach.

7.  Map $R \mapsto R^2$.

### Appendix: Data Generating Mechanism

Consider the linear additive model setup:

$$
Y = X^T\beta + \varepsilon
$$

where $X \sim N(0, \Sigma_{XX})$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ and $X \perp \varepsilon$.

Here, $X$ is a $p \times 1$ vector of predictors, $\Sigma_{XX}$​ is the predictor correlation matrix, and $\beta$ is a $p \times 1$ regression coefficient vector. True signal variables are defined by nonzero regression coefficients, while null/noise variables have coefficients equal to zero.

#### Population Joint Correlation/ Covariance Structure

The predictor correlation structure $R_{XX}$ is specified first. Given $R_{XX}, \beta$, and $\sigma^2$, the population joint covariance matrix of (Y,X) is $$
\Sigma =
\begin{bmatrix}
\Sigma_{YY} & \Sigma_{YX} \\
\Sigma_{XY} & \Sigma_{XX}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

where $$
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma_{YY} &= Var(Y)  \\ &= Var(X^T\beta + \varepsilon) \\ &= \beta^T\Sigma_{XX} \beta \ + \ \sigma^2
\\
\Sigma_{XY} &= Cov(X,Y) \\ &= Cov(X, X^T\beta + \varepsilon) \\&=  \Sigma_{XX}\beta
\end{aligned}
$$

If predictors are standardized, then $\Sigma_{XX}=R_{XX}$. The joint covariance matrix can then be converted to a joint correlation matrix. The MCMC perturbation procedure operates in this correlation space.
